deckTitle: Edexcel B A-Level Economics Theme 2 Flashcards
metaDescription: Free interactive flashcards for Edexcel B A-Level Economics Theme 2: business growth, elasticity, productive efficiency, the global economy, the economic cycle and macroeconomic policy, with spaced repetition.
intro: Revise Theme 2 with interactive flashcards written to the Edexcel B (9EB0) specification — business growth and competitive advantage, elasticities of demand, productive efficiency, life in a global economy, the economic cycle and macroeconomic policy. Flip each card to check yourself, rate how well you knew it, and the deck brings back the cards you found hard. Every card links to the revision notes page that teaches it.

cards.front: Define economies of scale and diseconomies of scale.
cards.back:
Economies of scale — the fall in long-run average cost that comes from producing on a larger scale.

Diseconomies of scale — the rise in long-run average cost when a firm grows beyond its minimum efficient scale.

Both are about average cost, the cost of each unit. A growing firm spends more in total, but if its output rises faster than its costs, each unit gets cheaper to make.

Diseconomies come from coordination problems, as more sites, departments and products are harder to plan and control, and weaker motivation, as each worker feels like a small part of a big organisation.

source.verbatim: the fall in long-run average cost that comes from producing on a larger scale.

cards.front: Distinguish internal from external economies of scale, with examples of each.
cards.back:
Internal economies of scale — cost savings that come from the growth of the firm itself.

  • Purchasing: bulk discounts on large orders.
  • Technical: large machinery whose cost is spread over far more units.
  • Financial: lenders see a large firm as safer, so it borrows at lower interest rates.
  • Managerial: specialist managers who make better decisions.
  • Marketing: an advert's cost per unit falls as sales rise.
  • Risk-bearing: a loss in one product or place is covered by profit in another.

External economies of scale — cost savings a firm gets from the growth of its whole industry, often in one area, not from its own size. Examples are a skilled labour pool, specialist suppliers nearby and better infrastructure.

Internal economies move a firm down its average cost curve. External economies shift the whole curve down, for large and small firms alike.

source.verbatim: cost savings that come from the growth of the firm itself.

cards.front: Define market power and market share. How does growth give a firm power over consumers and over suppliers?
cards.back:
Market power — a firm's ability to influence the prices it charges customers or pays suppliers.

Market share — one firm's sales as a percentage of the total sales in its market.

  • Over consumers: rivals shrink or disappear → fewer close substitutes → demand becomes more price inelastic → the firm can raise prices without losing many sales → higher profit, while consumers pay more and have less choice.
  • Over suppliers: the firm becomes one of a supplier's biggest customers → it negotiates lower prices or longer to pay → lower costs and better cash flow, while the supplier's margins are squeezed.

A bigger share usually brings brand recognition too: shoppers trust a name they see often, so they choose it first and their demand is less sensitive to price.

source.verbatim: a firm's ability to influence the prices it charges customers or pays suppliers.

cards.front: Define corporate culture. What role does it play as a firm grows?
cards.back:
Corporate culture — the shared values, attitudes and habits that shape how people in a business behave, often summed up as "the way we do things here".

  • It can hold a bigger firm together: staff share the same goals → fewer rules and checks are needed → decisions can be made lower down → faster, cheaper decisions and fewer communication problems.
  • It affects motivation: staff who feel trusted and valued work harder and stay longer.
  • Growth can weaken it: the founder can no longer know everyone → the old values fade → motivation falls → diseconomies of scale get worse.
  • Takeovers can bring a culture clash: conflict and senior staff leaving → the cost savings the deal promised do not arrive.

source.verbatim: the shared values, attitudes and habits that shape how people in a business behave, often summed up as "the way we do things here".

cards.front: Sketch the long-run average cost (LRAC) curve. Label economies of scale, diseconomies of scale and the minimum efficient scale.
cards.back:
Costs go up the side and quantity along the bottom. The LRAC curve is U-shaped.

  • On the left, average cost falls as output rises: economies of scale.
  • The lowest point marks the minimum efficient scale (MES) — the lowest output at which a firm reaches the lowest possible long-run average cost.
  • Beyond the MES, average cost rises again: diseconomies of scale.

A firm already at its MES gains no more cost savings from growing, and may start to face diseconomies.
cards.svgAlt: U-shaped long-run average cost curve (LRAC) with costs on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis; an arrow beside the falling left side is labelled economies of scale, an arrow beside the rising right side is labelled diseconomies of scale, and a dashed line from the lowest point of the curve marks MES on the quantity axis

source.verbatim: the lowest output at which a firm reaches the lowest possible long-run average cost.

cards.front: Evaluate whether growth will make a firm more profitable.
cards.back:
For

  • Economies of scale → lower average cost, and more market power → higher prices → a wider margin on each unit, and more units sold at that margin → higher total profit.

Against

  • Diseconomies of scale: coordination and motivation problems push average cost back up.
  • Internal communication: more layers of management → messages arrive late, changed or not at all → slow decisions and costly mistakes.
  • Skills shortages: the firm must outbid other employers for scarce staff, or hire less-skilled ones → higher labour costs, or slower output and more mistakes. The owner may lack the skills to run a bigger firm too.

Judgement: it depends on how close the firm is to its MES, and on whether the competition authorities step in: the CMA can block a merger or investigate a firm that uses its market power against consumers. How serious the problems are depends on the speed of growth, since a takeover can double a firm overnight, and on how the firm is organised, since regional or divisional managers keep chains of command short.

cards.front: Distinguish organic from inorganic growth. What is the difference between a merger and a takeover?
cards.back:
Organic growth — growth from within the business, using its own resources, such as selling more, launching new products or opening new sites. It is also called internal growth.

Inorganic growth — growth by joining with another business through a merger or a takeover. It is also called external growth.

  • A merger is when two firms agree to combine into one.
  • A takeover (or acquisition) is when one firm buys enough of another's shares, more than half, to control it.

source.verbatim: growth from within the business, using its own resources, such as selling more, launching new products or opening new sites. It is also called internal growth.

cards.front: Define integration, and distinguish horizontal, vertical and conglomerate integration.
cards.back:
Integration — two businesses coming together under one owner, through a merger or a takeover.

  • Horizontal integration — joining with a firm in the same industry at the same stage of production, usually a competitor.
  • Vertical integration — joining with a firm at a different stage of the same supply chain. It runs in two directions. Backward vertical integration is buying a supplier; forward vertical integration is buying a customer or outlet, closer to the consumer.
  • Conglomerate integration — joining with a firm in an unrelated market.

source.verbatim: two businesses coming together under one owner, through a merger or a takeover.

cards.front: Evaluate organic against inorganic growth. Which route is better for a firm?
cards.back:
Organic

  • Often paid for out of retained profit → little debt and no clash of cultures → lower risk, and the owners keep control.
  • But it is slow → a rival may win the market first, and the firm takes years to reach the scale where average cost is lowest.

Inorganic

  • Buying another firm brings instant market share and economies of scale: customers, staff and brands arrive at once.
  • But buyers usually pay above the firm's market value, often with borrowed money → interest costs rise. Paying with shares can dilute control, and if the two firms do not combine well, the promised savings never arrive.

Judgement: it depends on the finance available, since a small firm with modest profits may have no choice but to grow organically, and on how fast the market is moving, since in a fast-growing market waiting years to build up can mean losing it to rivals.

cards.front: Build the chain of reasoning: how does horizontal integration affect the firm, consumers and workers?
cards.back:
• The firm: two rivals become one → bigger orders and shared costs → economies of scale and a larger market share → lower average cost and more market power.
  • Consumers: one fewer competitor → less pressure on price → higher prices and less choice, unless the cost savings are passed on.
  • Workers: two head offices and two sales teams doing the same job → one is cut → job losses.

This is the type of integration the competition authorities watch most closely. In 2019 the CMA blocked a merger of Sainsbury's and Asda, finding it would lead to higher prices and lower quality and range for shoppers.

cards.front: A chocolate maker is planning a deal. Name the type of integration if it buys (a) a rival chocolate maker, (b) a cocoa supplier, (c) a chain of sweet shops or (d) a garden centre business. What should the analysis of each focus on?
cards.back:
• (a) Horizontal: the same industry at the same stage. Focus on market power: economies of scale and a bigger market share for the firm, but less competition for consumers.
  • (b) Backward vertical: a supplier at an earlier stage. Focus on control of the supply chain: a secure supply, control over quality and cost, and the profit the supplier used to make.
  • (c) Forward vertical: an outlet at a later stage, closer to the consumer. Focus on control of the supply chain: a guaranteed place to sell, and the shops' profit margin. The risk is running a business it does not know.
  • (d) Conglomerate: an unrelated market. Focus on spreading risk: a fall in chocolate sales no longer hits the whole business, but there are few shared savings and its managers know little about garden centres.

Name the type from what the two firms do. If the sweet shop chain bought the chocolate maker that supplies it, that would be backward vertical integration, not horizontal, even though both sell chocolate.

cards.front: Define research and development (R&D) and innovation. How is an invention different from an innovation?
cards.back:
Research and development (R&D) — the work a business does to discover new knowledge and turn it into new products or new ways of making them.

Innovation — turning a new idea into a product or process that is actually sold or used.

An invention is the idea itself. It only becomes an innovation when it reaches the market or the factory floor, and many inventions never do.

source.verbatim: the work a business does to discover new knowledge and turn it into new products or new ways of making them.

cards.front: Distinguish product innovation from process innovation. How does each give a firm a competitive advantage?
cards.back:
Product innovation — a new or improved good or service, such as a bakery launching a gluten-free range.

Process innovation — a new or improved way of producing or delivering a product, such as the same bakery installing ovens that bake twice as many loaves an hour.

  • Product: something rivals do not offer → the product is differentiated and demand becomes more price inelastic → the firm can charge a higher price → higher revenue and profit.
  • Process: output per worker or per machine rises → lower average cost → the firm can cut its price to win customers, or keep it and take a wider margin.

source.verbatim: a new or improved good or service, such as a bakery launching a gluten-free range.

cards.front: Define a patent. Build the chain from R&D to market power, and say how consumers gain and lose.
cards.back:
Patent — a legal right that lets an inventor take action against anyone who makes or sells their invention without permission. A UK patent lasts up to 20 years if it is renewed each year.

Successful R&D → the firm patents the result → rivals cannot sell a copy → the firm is the only supplier and can set a high price → high profits for the life of the patent. That prospect is the incentive to spend on risky R&D.

  • Consumers lose in the short run: one supplier → higher prices while the patent lasts.
  • Consumers gain in the long run: the profit pays for more R&D → new products that might not exist otherwise. When the patent ends, rivals enter and prices fall, as with cheaper copies of a medicine.

source.verbatim: a legal right that lets an inventor take action against anyone who makes or sells their invention without permission. A UK patent lasts up to 20 years if it is renewed each year.

cards.front: Evaluate state funding of R&D. Why do firms left to the market spend too little on it, and how well does government support work?
cards.back:
Why firms spend too little

  • Spillovers: new knowledge spreads to other firms and to consumers, who gain without paying. This is a positive externality, so the firm that pays for the research does not get all the benefit.
  • Risk: basic research may take decades to pay off, or never pay off at all.

For

  • Tax relief and grants → R&D costs firms less → more projects are worth doing → more innovation → higher productivity and economic growth.

Against

  • Choosing well: officials may back projects that fail, and have less at stake than an investor using their own money.
  • Paying for what would have happened anyway: if a firm would have done the research without help, the subsidy just adds to its profit.

Judgement: left to the market, firms spend less on R&D than is best for society, so there is a case for support. How well it works depends on backing the right projects, and on funding research that would not have happened without it.

cards.front: Sketch the product life cycle. Label the four stages and show an extension strategy. What happens to sales and profit at each stage?
cards.back:
Product life cycle — the stages a product's sales pass through over time, from launch to withdrawal.

Sales go up the side and time along the bottom.

  • Introduction: sales are low, as few customers know the product. Usually a loss, as R&D and launch costs are still being paid.
  • Growth: sales rise fast. Profit appears and cash flow turns positive, and rivals start to enter.
  • Maturity: sales are high but level off. Profit is highest, as costs are spread over high sales.
  • Decline: sales fall as tastes change or better products arrive, and profit falls.

An extension strategy branches off just after decline begins and lifts sales again.
cards.svgAlt: Product life cycle with sales on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis; the sales curve starts at zero, rises slowly through introduction, steeply through growth, levels off and peaks in maturity, and falls in decline, with dashed lines marking where each stage ends; just after decline begins, a second curve labelled extension strategy branches off and lifts sales back above their earlier peak

source.verbatim: the stages a product's sales pass through over time, from launch to withdrawal.

cards.front: Define an extension strategy, and give four examples. When is one worth it?
cards.back:
Extension strategy — action taken to lengthen a product's life by lifting sales when they level off or start to fall.

  • New markets: selling abroad or to a new type of customer.
  • Repackaging or redesign: a new look, size or version that makes the product feel new.
  • New uses: finding another reason to buy it.
  • Price changes: a price cut or promotion to win back price-sensitive buyers.

Sales rise again → more revenue from a product whose development is already paid for → cash to fund the next new product.

It is worth it only if the reason sales are falling can be fixed, since a new pack will not save a product that newer technology has replaced, and if the same budget would not earn more spent on a new product.

source.verbatim: action taken to lengthen a product's life by lifting sales when they level off or start to fall.

cards.front: Define viral marketing and micromarketing. How does each help a firm?
cards.back:
Viral marketing — marketing designed to be shared by the people who see it, so it spreads from person to person at little cost to the firm.

A video that goes viral reaches millions for the cost of making it, which lets a small firm compete with big advertising budgets. The catch is that nobody can be sure what will spread.

Micromarketing — targeting very small groups of customers, or individuals, with products and offers tailored to them, using data on what they search for and buy.

Data shows what each customer wants → offers matched to them → more of them buy, and less is wasted on adverts nobody needs → higher sales per pound spent on marketing.

source.verbatim: marketing designed to be shared by the people who see it, so it spreads from person to person at little cost to the firm.

cards.front: Define a price comparison site. Build the chain: how do these sites affect consumers and firms?
cards.back:
Price comparison site — a website that lists the prices of the same product from many sellers side by side, used for things such as energy, flights and broadband.

  • Consumers: comparing prices takes seconds → buyers find the cheapest seller → lower prices paid and more chance of switching.
  • Firms: demand becomes more price elastic → a small price rise loses many sales → firms must compete on price → margins are squeezed, and the lowest-cost firms win.

A standard product is judged on price alone, while a strong brand or a niche product keeps some pricing power.

source.verbatim: a website that lists the prices of the same product from many sellers side by side, used for things such as energy, flights and broadband.

cards.front: Sketch the long tail. Why can an online seller profit from it when a shop cannot?
cards.back:
Long tail — the large number of niche products that each sell only a few units, but together can make up a big share of sales.

Sales go up the side and products, ranked by sales, along the bottom. The curve falls steeply across the head, a few best-sellers, then flattens into a long, low tail of niche products, shaded to show that together they add up.

A shop has room for only so many products, so it stocks the best-sellers. An online seller can list millions, because a listing costs almost nothing to keep. Each niche product sells only a few units, but together they add up, and customers with unusual tastes find what they want.
cards.svgAlt: The long tail, with sales on the vertical axis and products ranked by sales on the horizontal axis; the curve falls steeply across the first few products, labelled head: a few best-sellers, then flattens into a long, low tail running to the right, which is shaded and labelled long tail: many niche products

source.verbatim: the large number of niche products that each sell only a few units, but together can make up a big share of sales.

cards.front: Define network effects. Why does the digital economy create many new firms, yet let a few platforms dominate?
cards.back:
Network effects — when a product becomes more useful to each user as more people use it.

  • Creation: start-up costs are low → a laptop and a website can be enough to start trading → many new firms enter → more choice for consumers and new jobs.
  • Destruction: customers move online → high-street shops, travel agents and bank branches lose custom → closures and job losses.
  • Dominance: a marketplace with more sellers attracts more buyers → more buyers attract more sellers → the platform keeps growing → it can come to dominate its market, and a new rival struggles to attract either side.

So barriers to entry are lower, but network effects let a few online platforms grow very large.

source.verbatim: when a product becomes more useful to each user as more people use it.

cards.front: Evaluate whether the digital economy raises a firm's profit.
cards.back:
For

  • Lower costs: no shop rent, cheaper marketing and near-free distribution of digital products → lower average cost.
  • Wider markets: a website can be seen anywhere → customers across the country or abroad → more sales, and economies of scale a local market could never support.

Against

  • Lower prices: price comparison and rivals from anywhere → more price-elastic demand → lower prices.
  • New costs: warehouses, delivery, returns, the website and its security, and scarce staff with digital skills.

Judgement: profit rises for firms whose costs fall faster than their prices, and turns to loss for those whose prices fall faster. It depends on whether the product can be sold online, since a hairdresser is barely affected while a seller of books, music or insurance is transformed, and on how differentiated it is.

cards.front: Define a unique selling point (USP). Build the chain: how does a USP help a small firm survive against larger rivals?
cards.back:
Unique selling point (USP) — a feature of a product or business that customers value and rivals do not offer.

Something customers cannot get elsewhere → fewer close substitutes → demand is more price inelastic → the firm can charge more than larger rivals without losing many sales → a margin high enough to survive on.

A small firm needs this because large rivals have economies of scale, so their average cost is usually lower, and matching their prices would mean a loss.

source.verbatim: a feature of a product or business that customers value and rivals do not offer.

cards.front: Define a niche market. Why does targeting one suit a small firm, and what are the risks?
cards.back:
Niche market — a small, clearly defined part of a larger market, with its own particular needs.

Specialising lets a small firm become the expert. The niche is often too small for a large firm to bother with → little direct competition → loyal customers willing to pay a premium.

Risks: the niche can shrink if tastes change, and a niche that grows can attract a large firm that brings its lower costs with it.

source.verbatim: a small, clearly defined part of a larger market, with its own particular needs.

cards.front: Build the chains of reasoning: how do flexibility and customer service help a small firm compete?
cards.back:
• Flexibility: few layers of management, often just the owner → a customer asks for something unusual → the owner decides on the spot → the order is met within days → sales that a large firm's fixed range and procedures would miss. The range can change quickly too, while a chain waits for a decision from head office.
  • Customer service: customers deal with the owner, who knows their names and what they bought last time → they feel valued → they come back and recommend the firm to friends → repeat sales and free word-of-mouth advertising, from customers who are less likely to switch for a lower price.

cards.front: An independent café competes with a national coffee chain. Apply relationships with stakeholders: how could its suppliers, employees and local community each give it an advantage?
cards.back:
• Suppliers: a long-standing local bakery → quick deliveries, help in a rush and sometimes longer to pay → lower stock costs and better cash flow.
  • Employees: a small team that knows the owner and the regulars → higher motivation and fewer staff leaving → lower recruitment costs and better service.
  • Local community: the café sponsors a local running club → goodwill and loyalty from people who want to support local businesses → more sales.

Close relationships like these are a competitive advantage that size cannot buy, and a chain finds personal service and local ties hard to copy.

cards.front: Evaluate whether a small firm can survive against large rivals without competing on price.
cards.back:
Why not compete on price? Large rivals have economies of scale and lower average cost. A small firm that tries to match their prices will make a loss, and cannot win a price war.

For

  • A USP, flexibility, personal service, a niche and close stakeholder relationships all give customers a reason to pay a little more.

Against

  • Copying: a large chain can copy an extra such as a free service, though it finds personal service and local ties harder to copy.
  • The cost gap: customers pay a little more for service, but not much more. If the chain's prices are far lower, many will switch.

Judgement: it depends on the size of the cost gap. In trades where economies of scale are small, such as hairdressing, the gap may hardly exist. Where it is large, the small firm needs an advantage that a large rival would find hard to copy.

cards.topic: 2.2 Firms, Consumers and Elasticities of Demand
cards.front: Define price elasticity of demand (PED). What makes demand for a product more price elastic?
cards.back:
Price elasticity of demand (PED) — how much the quantity demanded of a product responds to a change in its own price.

Demand is more price elastic when:

  • There are more, and closer, substitutes: customers can switch easily when the price rises. This is the most important factor.
  • The product is a luxury, not a necessity.
  • It takes a large share of income: a 10% rise in the price of a car is noticed far more than a 10% rise in the price of salt.
  • Customers have more time to respond: in the short run people are stuck with their habits, but over time they find alternatives.
  • The market is defined narrowly: demand for petrol is price inelastic, but demand for petrol from one filling station is price elastic, because the next one is a short drive away.

Demand is more price inelastic where buyers are loyal to a brand or the product is habit-forming.

source.verbatim: how much the quantity demanded of a product responds to a change in its own price.

cards.topic: 2.2 Firms, Consumers and Elasticities of Demand
cards.front: State the formula for PED. Why is the answer negative, and how do you classify the value?
cards.back:
Work out each percentage change from the original figure, then divide. Price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions, so the answer is negative.

Ignore the minus sign when you classify. What matters is the size of the number:

  • 0: perfectly inelastic. Quantity demanded does not change at all.
  • Between 0 and 1: price inelastic. Quantity changes by a smaller percentage than price.
  • 1: unitary elastic. Quantity changes by the same percentage as price.
  • Greater than 1: price elastic. Quantity changes by a larger percentage than price.
  • Infinite: perfectly elastic. Any rise in price and sales fall to zero.

The number also gives the size of the response: a PED of −0.5 means a 10% price rise cuts quantity demanded by 5%.
cards.formula: \text{PED} = \frac{\%\text{ change in quantity demanded}}{\%\text{ change in price}}

cards.topic: 2.2 Firms, Consumers and Elasticities of Demand
cards.front:
A cinema raises its ticket price from £8 to £10. Weekly attendance falls from 2,000 to 1,800.

Calculate the PED and the change in weekly total revenue. Is demand price elastic or price inelastic?
cards.back:
• % change in quantity demanded: (1,800 − 2,000) ÷ 2,000 × 100 = −10%.
  • % change in price: (10 − 8) ÷ 8 × 100 = +25%.
  • PED: −10 ÷ +25 = −0.4.
  • Total revenue: £8 × 2,000 = £16,000 before and £10 × 1,800 = £18,000 after, a rise of £2,000.

Ignoring the sign, 0.4 is less than 1, so demand is price inelastic: attendance fell by a smaller percentage than the price rose. The higher price outweighs the lost sales, so total revenue rises.

cards.topic: 2.2 Firms, Consumers and Elasticities of Demand
cards.front: Define total revenue. Build the chain: how does PED decide what a price rise does to total revenue?
cards.back:
Total revenue — the money a firm receives from selling its product (also called sales revenue). Total revenue = price × quantity sold.

A price rise means more money on each unit but fewer units sold. PED tells you which effect wins.

  • Price inelastic: price rises 10% → sales fall by less than 10% → the higher price outweighs the lost sales → total revenue rises.
  • Price elastic: price rises 10% → sales fall by more than 10% → the lost sales outweigh the higher price → total revenue falls.
  • Unitary elastic: the two effects cancel out → total revenue stays the same.

A price cut works the other way round. Higher revenue is not the same as higher profit: before recommending a price cut, check what the extra units cost to make.

source.verbatim: the money a firm receives from selling its product (also called sales revenue)

cards.topic: 2.2 Firms, Consumers and Elasticities of Demand
cards.front: Explain why PED usually differs between a mass market and a niche market. Evaluate how useful PED is when a firm sets its price.
cards.back:
Mass market — a large market in which many firms sell similar products to customers with broadly the same needs.

  • Mass market: many rivals sell near-identical products → customers have plenty of close substitutes → demand for one firm's product is price elastic → a price rise loses so many sales that revenue falls. Firms price close to their rivals and rely on high volume at a low margin.
  • Niche market: a specialist product with few substitutes and loyal buyers → demand is price inelastic → the firm can charge a premium and lose few sales → a high margin on a low volume.

How useful is PED?

  • Rivals react: in a mass market, a price cut that rivals match wins few extra sales, so revenue falls for everyone.
  • The estimate may be out of date: PED is worked out from past sales, while tastes, incomes and rivals' prices keep changing. It also holds only for small price changes.

Judgement: PED is a guide, not a forecast. It is most reliable for a small price change that rivals are unlikely to match, and least reliable in a mass market where a price cut is quickly copied. This is why firms work to make demand more price inelastic, through branding and other non-price competition.

source.verbatim: a large market in which many firms sell similar products to customers with broadly the same needs.

cards.topic: 2.2 Firms, Consumers and Elasticities of Demand
cards.front: Define price skimming and penetration pricing. When does each suit a new product?
cards.back:
Price skimming — launching a new product at a high price, then lowering it over time.

High launch price → a large margin on each sale to the keenest early buyers → R&D costs are recovered quickly → later price cuts bring in more cautious buyers. It needs a product rivals cannot copy straight away, often protected by a patent. Risks: the high profit attracts rivals, and early buyers may resent a quick price cut.

Penetration pricing — launching at a low price to win market share quickly, then raising it.

Low launch price → customers try the product and switch from rivals → market share and higher output → economies of scale lower unit cost. It suits a mass market where demand is price elastic. Risks: low profit or losses at first, and customers leaving when the price goes up.

source.verbatim: launching a new product at a high price, then lowering it over time.

cards.topic: 2.2 Firms, Consumers and Elasticities of Demand
cards.front: Define predatory pricing, competitive pricing and psychological pricing.
cards.back:
Predatory pricing — setting a price below cost to force rivals out of the market, then raising it.

Price below cost → rivals make losses and leave → less competition → the firm raises prices and recovers its losses. Only a large firm with the cash to survive the losses can do this, and it is illegal when a dominant firm uses it.

Competitive pricing — setting a price at or close to rivals' prices.

The norm where products are similar and customers compare prices. Charging more loses sales and charging less may start a price war, so firms compete on service, location and brand instead.

Psychological pricing — setting a price for its effect on how customers see the product.

A price of £4.99 reads as "£4 and something" → it feels much cheaper than £5 → more sales. It can work the other way too: a high, round price signals quality and status.

source.verbatim: setting a price below cost to force rivals out of the market, then raising it.

cards.topic: 2.2 Firms, Consumers and Elasticities of Demand
cards.front:
A candle maker spends £3 on wax and £4 on labour for each candle, and adds £1 per candle to cover overheads. It uses a 50% mark-up.

Calculate its selling price. A rival sells a candle for £15 that costs £12 to make: what is the rival's mark-up?
cards.back:
Cost-plus pricing — adding a percentage mark-up to the cost of making each unit to set the price.

  • Unit cost: £3 + £4 + £1 = £8.
  • Mark-up: 50% × £8 = £4.
  • Selling price: £8 + £4 = £12.
  • Rival's mark-up: (£15 − £12) ÷ £12 × 100 = 25%.

A mark-up is a percentage of cost, not of price. The £4 mark-up is 50% of the £8 cost, but only 33.3% of the £12 price (4 ÷ 12 × 100). Dividing by the price gives the profit margin instead, a different figure.

Cost-plus makes sure each sale covers its cost, but it ignores demand and rivals' prices. The £1 overhead share also assumes a set number of sales: with fewer, each candle carries more of the overheads.

source.verbatim: adding a percentage mark-up to the cost of making each unit to set the price.

cards.topic: 2.2 Firms, Consumers and Elasticities of Demand
cards.front: Define a pricing strategy. Evaluate what decides which strategy is most appropriate for a firm.
cards.back:
Pricing strategy — the approach a firm takes to setting the price of a product over time.

  • USPs and differentiation: a product with features rivals lack can be skimmed or priced at a premium. A standard product has to be priced competitively.
  • PED: price inelastic demand supports skimming and higher prices. Price elastic demand favours penetration or competitive pricing, because a price cut wins many extra sales.
  • Amount of competition: with many close rivals, the firm has little choice but to match their prices. With few, it has room to set its own.
  • Strength of brand: a well-known brand can charge more than rivals and keep its customers.
  • Stage in the product life cycle: skimming or penetration at launch, competitive pricing in maturity, and price cuts to clear stock in decline.
  • Costs: in the long run the price has to cover unit cost. A small firm cannot afford months of penetration or predatory losses that a large firm can absorb.

Judgement: no strategy suits every case, and the factors work together. A differentiated product with few rivals has price inelastic demand and room to price high, by skimming at launch or charging a premium later, while a standard product in a crowded market is pushed into competitive pricing. The firm's costs and cash then limit how long it can afford to price low.

source.verbatim: the approach a firm takes to setting the price of a product over time.

cards.topic: 2.2 Firms, Consumers and Elasticities of Demand
cards.front: Build the chain of reasoning: how have online sales and price comparison sites changed the way firms set prices?
cards.back:
• Sellers of standard products: shoppers see every price in seconds → demand for each seller becomes more price elastic → firms are pushed into competitive pricing → lower margins and profit.
  • Online retailers: no shops to rent or staff → lower costs → lower prices → high-street rivals lose sales unless they match the price or give a reason to pay more.
  • Firms that change prices often: online prices cost nothing to change → airlines and hotels raise them when demand is high and cut them when it is low → more revenue from the same seats and rooms.

Firms respond by making their prices harder to compare: bundles, versions sold through only one retailer, and loyalty-card prices.

How much this matters depends on how easy the product is to compare, as broadband deals are compared mainly on price and a haircut is not, and on brand loyalty, as loyal customers may not look at a comparison site at all.

cards.topic: 2.2 Firms, Consumers and Elasticities of Demand
cards.front: Define non-price competition and marketing. Why might a firm compete this way rather than cut its price?
cards.back:
Non-price competition — winning customers through anything other than a lower price, such as quality, branding, advertising or where the product is sold.

Marketing — finding out what customers want and persuading them to buy the firm's product.

A price cut is easy for rivals to copy and lowers the margin on every unit. Non-price competition is harder to copy, and if it works the firm can keep its price, or raise it.

The spec names three ways to do it: product differentiation, advertising and other promotion, and distribution.

source.verbatim: winning customers through anything other than a lower price, such as quality, branding, advertising or where the product is sold.

cards.topic: 2.2 Firms, Consumers and Elasticities of Demand
cards.front: Build the chain of reasoning: what two effects does successful marketing have on a product's demand curve, and why does revenue rise?
cards.back:
• Demand shifts to the right: more customers know about the product and want it → more is demanded at every price → higher sales without a price cut.
  • Demand becomes more price inelastic: customers see the product as different from, and better than, its rivals → fewer close substitutes in their eyes → the demand curve becomes steeper → the firm can raise its price and lose few sales.

Together they mean higher sales at a higher price, so revenue rises.

Name both effects. A shift to the right is only half the answer. The change in elasticity is what lets the firm raise its price without losing many sales: link it to margins and profit.

cards.topic: 2.2 Firms, Consumers and Elasticities of Demand
cards.front: Define promotion. How do informative and persuasive advertising affect demand, and what other promotional methods can a firm use?
cards.back:
Promotion — communicating with customers to make them aware of a product and persuade them to buy it.

  • Informative advertising: tells customers the product exists, what it does and where to get it → more buyers → demand shifts right.
  • Persuasive advertising: builds a brand image customers identify with → brand loyalty → buyers stick with the product when its price rises → demand becomes more price inelastic.

Other methods: sales promotions such as free samples and loyalty schemes, sponsorship, social media and influencers, and public relations, the free coverage in news stories and reviews that customers often trust more than an advert.

source.verbatim: communicating with customers to make them aware of a product and persuade them to buy it.

cards.topic: 2.2 Firms, Consumers and Elasticities of Demand
cards.front: Define distribution. How can a firm's choice of distribution method change demand and its margin?
cards.back:
Distribution — how a product gets from the producer to the customer, and where customers can buy it.

A firm can sell direct, through its own shops or website, or through intermediaries, such as wholesalers and retailers that stock its products.

  • Wider distribution: a listing in a national supermarket chain → customers find the product on every shopping trip → demand shifts right. The supermarket takes a share of the price, so the margin on each unit falls.
  • Selling direct online: no retailer's cut → a higher margin, and the firm sees exactly who its customers are → it can target them with offers. It pays for delivery and returns instead.
  • Selective distribution: selling only through its own stores and a few chosen retailers → the product looks exclusive → demand becomes more price inelastic → a premium price.

source.verbatim: how a product gets from the producer to the customer, and where customers can buy it.

cards.topic: 2.2 Firms, Consumers and Elasticities of Demand
cards.front: Evaluate how a firm should choose its marketing approach, and whether spending on promotion will pay.
cards.back:
There is no single best approach. A national breakfast cereal brand needs national advertising and the widest possible distribution. A small maker of handmade dog treats relies on its story, social media and a few specialist shops, and charges a premium.

The right approach depends on:

  • The target market: who the customers are, what they value and where they shop, found through market research and segmentation.
  • The product: a complex product needs advertising that explains what it does. A low-priced impulse buy needs to be on as many shelves as possible.
  • The budget: a small firm cannot match a large rival's advertising, so it leans on differentiation, service and social media.
  • Stage in the product life cycle: informative advertising at launch, persuasive advertising and brand building in maturity, and extension strategies as sales fall.

Will promotion pay? Not if it costs more than the extra sales bring in, as a television campaign can for a small firm. And if every firm in the market advertises, each may just hold on to its share while all of them pay higher costs.

Judgement: the best approach is the one that fits the firm's customers, product and budget. Promotion pays only when the extra revenue is greater than its cost, which is hardest where every rival is advertising too.

cards.topic: 2.2 Firms, Consumers and Elasticities of Demand
cards.front: Define income elasticity of demand (YED). What decides whether a product's YED is high, low or negative?
cards.back:
Income elasticity of demand (YED) — how much the quantity demanded of a product responds to a change in consumers' real income.

Real income is income adjusted for inflation. It rises when the economy grows and can fall in a recession.

  • How essential the product is: necessities have low YED, because people buy them whatever their income. Luxuries have high YED.
  • The customer's income level: the same product can be a luxury for a low-income household and a necessity for a high-income one. As a country gets richer, goods such as cars move from one group to the other.
  • Whether better alternatives exist: a product is inferior when people swap it for something they prefer as they earn more, such as bus travel for a car.

source.verbatim: how much the quantity demanded of a product responds to a change in consumers' real income.

cards.topic: 2.2 Firms, Consumers and Elasticities of Demand
cards.front: Define a normal good and an inferior good. What YED values show a luxury, a necessity and an inferior good?
cards.back:
Normal good — a product whose demand rises when income rises, so YED is positive.

Inferior good — a product whose demand falls when income rises, so YED is negative.

  • Greater than 1: a luxury (normal, income elastic), such as holidays and meals out. When incomes fall, sales fall by a larger percentage than income.
  • Between 0 and 1: a necessity (normal, income inelastic), such as bread and electricity. When incomes fall, sales fall a little.
  • Less than 0: inferior, such as budget brands and bus travel. When incomes fall, sales rise.

Always keep the sign of YED. With PED you drop the minus sign, but with YED it is the answer: −0.6 shows an inferior good, and +0.6 a necessity. "Inferior" is about how demand reacts to income, not about quality.

source.verbatim: a product whose demand rises when income rises, so YED is positive.

cards.topic: 2.2 Firms, Consumers and Elasticities of Demand
cards.front: State the formula for YED. In a recession, real incomes fall by 4%. Sales of a supermarket's budget range rise by 2%, and sales of package holidays fall by 10%. Calculate the YED of each and name the type of good.
cards.back:
• Budget range: +2 ÷ −4 = −0.5. Negative, so an inferior good: shoppers trade down as their incomes fall.
  • Package holidays: −10 ÷ −4 = +2.5. Positive and greater than 1, so a normal good and a luxury: sales fell 2.5 times as fast as income.

Watch the signs when income falls. Sales falling with income gives a positive YED, a normal good. Sales rising as income falls gives a negative YED, an inferior good.
cards.formula: \text{YED} = \frac{\%\text{ change in quantity demanded}}{\%\text{ change in real income}}

cards.topic: 2.2 Firms, Consumers and Elasticities of Demand
cards.front: Build the chain of reasoning: how does YED tell a firm what the economic cycle will do to its sales?
cards.back:
• Sellers of luxuries in a boom: real incomes rise → demand grows faster than income → sales and profit rise → the firm hires staff and invests in extra capacity.
  • Sellers of luxuries in a recession: real incomes fall → customers cut back on luxuries first → sales fall sharply → lower profit, and jobs at risk.
  • Sellers of inferior goods in a recession: shoppers trade down → demand rises → discount retailers and budget brands gain sales and market share.
  • Sellers of necessities: demand barely moves either way → steady sales through the cycle.

cards.topic: 2.2 Firms, Consumers and Elasticities of Demand
cards.front: Evaluate how useful YED is to a firm planning its products and output.
cards.back:
For

  • A product portfolio: a firm with both a premium range and a budget range sells more of one when it sells less of the other → steadier total sales across the economic cycle.
  • Output and stock: a firm expecting a downturn can order fewer of its luxuries and more of its inferior goods, as a car dealer might order fewer new cars and more used ones.

Against

  • The estimate may be wrong: YED is worked out from past data, and tastes change.
  • Whose income is changing: average income can rise while the firm's own customers are worse off.

Judgement: YED shows which way, and roughly how strongly, a firm's sales will move over the cycle. How far the firm can rely on it depends on how recent the estimate is and on whether its own customers' incomes are moving with the average.

cards.front: Define productivity and labour productivity. Why is productivity not the same as output?
cards.back:
Productivity — output per unit of input in a given time period.

Labour productivity — output per worker, or per hour worked, in a given period.

Output per hour is fairer when staff work different hours, and it is the measure usually quoted for the UK economy.

Productivity is not output. A firm that hires more staff can raise its output while each worker makes no more than before. Productivity only rises when each worker, or each hour, produces more.

source.verbatim: output per unit of input in a given time period.

cards.front:
A call centre's 12 staff handle 1,440 calls a day, and each is paid £120 a day. New software lets the same 12 staff handle 1,800 calls.

Calculate labour productivity and the unit labour cost of a call, before and after. If the centre had instead hired a 13th worker and handled 1,560 calls, what would productivity be?
cards.back:
Unit labour cost is the labour cost of making one unit: the wage bill divided by output.

  • Before: 1,440 ÷ 12 = 120 calls per worker a day. The wage bill is 12 × £120 = £1,440, so unit labour cost is £1,440 ÷ 1,440 = £1.00 a call.
  • After: 1,800 ÷ 12 = 150 calls per worker a day. Unit labour cost is £1,440 ÷ 1,800 = 80p a call.
  • A 13th worker: 1,560 ÷ 13 = 120 calls. Output has risen, but productivity has not.

Higher productivity at the same wage lowers unit labour cost, which is why it matters for competitiveness. Hiring more staff raises output without making each worker any more productive.

cards.front: Define competitiveness. Build the chain of reasoning from higher productivity to a more competitive firm, and say what limits the gain.
cards.back:
Competitiveness — a firm's ability to win sales from its rivals, on price or on quality.

  • The firm: more output per worker → lower unit labour cost → lower average cost → it can cut prices to win sales, or keep them and earn a wider margin.
  • Exporters: lower unit costs → UK goods can be priced below overseas rivals' → more export sales.

The gain depends on:

  • Wages: if pay rises as fast as productivity, unit labour cost does not fall.
  • Rivals' productivity: competitiveness is relative. A firm whose productivity improves by 2% a year still falls behind rivals improving by 5%.

source.verbatim: a firm's ability to win sales from its rivals, on price or on quality.

cards.front: Explain why rising productivity matters for economic growth and for wages. Evaluate whether workers always share in a productivity gain.
cards.back:
Economic growth — an increase in real GDP, the value of an economy's output adjusted for inflation.

  • Growth: productivity rises across the economy → more output from the same workers → the economy's productive potential grows → higher real incomes, and more tax revenue for the government. The workforce grows slowly, so lasting rises in living standards depend on productivity.
  • Wages: each worker produces more → their work is worth more to the firm → it can raise pay and keep unit labour cost the same → higher real wages.

Do workers always gain?

  • Bargaining power: when staff are hard to find, or a trade union is strong, workers can push for a share. Otherwise the firm may keep the gain as profit.
  • Where the gain came from: if a machine now does work people used to do, output per worker rises but some jobs go.
  • Pay that outruns productivity: unit labour cost rises → the firm raises prices or accepts lower profit, and may cut jobs.

Judgement: higher productivity makes higher real wages possible, not certain. Workers are most likely to share in it when labour is scarce and the gain does not come from replacing staff with machines. The link also runs the other way: better pay can raise productivity, because motivated staff work harder and fewer leave.

source.verbatim: an increase in real GDP, the value of an economy's output adjusted for inflation

cards.front: Define labour-intensive and capital-intensive production. How do they differ, and what decides which one a firm uses?
cards.back:
Labour-intensive production — production that uses a high proportion of labour compared with capital, so wages are a large share of costs.

Capital-intensive production — production that uses a high proportion of machinery and equipment compared with labour.

  • Costs: a labour-intensive firm's biggest cost is wages. A capital-intensive firm's is machinery, mostly a fixed cost, so it needs high output to keep average cost down.
  • Labour productivity: higher in capital-intensive production, as each worker has more capital to use.
  • Flexibility: labour-intensive production can change the product or cut hours easily. Machines suit long runs of one standard product.

The choice depends on the cost of labour against capital (as wages rise, firms switch to machines, such as self-service tills), the scale of output, and the product: personal training needs people.

source.verbatim: production that uses a high proportion of labour compared with capital, so wages are a large share of costs.

cards.front: Define capacity, full capacity and spare capacity.
cards.back:
Capacity — the most a firm can produce in a given period with its existing premises, machinery and staff.

Full capacity — producing at that maximum, with no resources standing idle.

Spare capacity — the gap between what a firm produces and the most it could produce. The firm could raise output by this much without new premises or machinery.

A climbing wall can take 40 climbers a session. With all 40 places booked it is at full capacity. With 25 booked, it has spare capacity of 15 places.

source.verbatim: the most a firm can produce in a given period with its existing premises, machinery and staff.

cards.front:
A factory can make 6,000 garden chairs a month. Its fixed costs are £27,000 a month, materials cost £10 a chair, and each chair sells for £17.

Calculate capacity utilisation, fixed cost per chair and average cost when it makes 3,000 chairs, and when it makes 5,400. What is the profit or loss on each chair?
cards.back:
Capacity utilisation — the firm's current output as a percentage of its maximum possible output.

  • 3,000 chairs: CU = 3,000 ÷ 6,000 × 100 = 50%. Fixed cost per chair = £27,000 ÷ 3,000 = £9. Average cost = £9 + £10 = £19, a loss of £2 on each chair.
  • 5,400 chairs: CU = 5,400 ÷ 6,000 × 100 = 90%. Fixed cost per chair = £27,000 ÷ 5,400 = £5. Average cost = £5 + £10 = £15, a profit of £2 on each chair.

Only the fixed cost per unit changes. Materials cost £10 a chair at 50% or at 90%. Say that fixed costs are spread over more units, and show it with the figures.

source.verbatim: the firm's current output as a percentage of its maximum possible output

cards.front: Build the chains of reasoning: what goes wrong when a firm's capacity utilisation is too low, and when it is too high?
cards.back:
Under-utilisation (a lot of spare capacity):

  • Unit costs: low output → fixed costs are spread over fewer units → higher average cost → higher prices or lower margins → less competitive.
  • Staff: quiet shifts and idle machines → workers worry about their jobs → lower motivation and productivity.

Over-utilisation (at or near full capacity):

  • Machinery: no time for maintenance → more breakdowns → lost output and repair bills.
  • Staff: long hours and overtime → tiredness and mistakes → lower quality, and higher wage costs from overtime pay.
  • Customers: extra orders are turned down → customers go to rivals → lost sales that may not come back.

So most firms aim for a high rate of utilisation that stops short of 100%.

cards.front: A firm is running at 55% capacity utilisation. Evaluate how serious a problem this is.
cards.back:
Why it matters: rent, machinery and salaried staff cost the same whether the firm is busy or quiet → fixed costs are spread over fewer units → higher average cost → thinner margins, or higher prices.

It depends on:

  • How long it lasts: a ski-hire shop expects to be quiet in summer and plans for it. Low utilisation all year round means the firm has more capacity than it needs.
  • The share of fixed costs: for airlines, hotels and cinemas, each empty seat or room pushes average cost up a lot. A firm whose costs are mostly variable is hit far less.
  • Some spare capacity is useful: the firm can take a large order at short notice, and has time to maintain machines and train staff.

Judgement: 55% is most serious for a firm with high fixed costs that expects demand to stay low, which needs to fill its capacity or cut it. A seasonal dip at a firm whose costs are mostly variable matters far less.

cards.front: Define rationalisation. What are the two routes to higher capacity utilisation, and what does each cost the firm?
cards.back:
Rationalisation — cutting capacity to match demand, for example by closing a site, selling machinery, cutting shifts or making staff redundant.

  • Raise output to fill capacity: increase demand through marketing, new markets or lower prices at quiet times, or make something else, using idle machines for a new product or working as a subcontractor for other firms. The cost: a price cut lowers revenue per unit, and only raises revenue if demand is price elastic.
  • Cut capacity to match output: fewer premises, machines and staff → lower fixed costs → higher utilisation and lower average cost at the same output. The cost: redundancy payments, lower morale among the staff who stay, and if demand recovers, the firm may not be able to meet it.

An over-utilised firm does the opposite. It adds capacity by buying machinery or running an extra shift, or outsources work to other firms. Adding capacity only makes sense if the extra demand is expected to last.

source.verbatim: cutting capacity to match demand, for example by closing a site, selling machinery, cutting shifts or making staff redundant.

cards.front: Define lean production and quality. Which methods does lean production use?
cards.back:
Lean production — an approach to production that aims to cut waste of every kind, such as materials, time, stock and faulty products, while keeping quality high.

Quality — how well a product meets customers' expectations, every time they buy it.

Each lean method is a way of making the same output with fewer resources, in services as well as manufacturing:

  • Managing quality: quality control, quality assurance and Total Quality Management (TQM).
  • Continuous improvement: Kaizen.
  • Stock management: just-in-time (JIT).

source.verbatim: an approach to production that aims to cut waste of every kind, such as materials, time, stock and faulty products, while keeping quality high.

cards.front: Define quality control, quality assurance and Total Quality Management (TQM). When is a fault found under each, and by whom?
cards.back:
Quality control — checking finished products, or samples of them, and rejecting any that are faulty.

Quality assurance — setting standards for each stage of production and checking work against them as it is done, so faults are stopped before the product is finished.

Total Quality Management (TQM) — making quality the responsibility of every employee in every department, with each stage of the work treating the next as its customer.

  • Quality control: after the product is made, by inspectors. Faulty products have already used up materials and time.
  • Quality assurance: at each stage of production, by workers checking their own work. Setting and checking the standards costs time.
  • TQM: faults are prevented at source, by everyone, including staff who never see the product. It needs training and a change of culture, which are slow.

Control finds faults; assurance stops them being made. If staff check their own work at each stage, that is assurance, and the saving comes from less waste, not from better inspection.

source.verbatim: setting standards for each stage of production and checking work against them as it is done, so faults are stopped before the product is finished.

cards.front: Define Kaizen. How does it lower a firm's costs, and when does it work less well?
cards.back:
Kaizen — continuous improvement through many small, regular changes, most of them suggested by the workers who do the job.

In a warehouse, moving the most-ordered items next to the packing bench saves a few steps on every order.

  • Costs: small changes, made constantly → less wasted time, movement and materials → higher productivity → lower average cost.
  • Staff: workers' ideas are put into practice → they feel involved → higher motivation and fewer staff leaving.

It works less well when:

  • A big change is needed: small steps cannot keep up with a rival that brings in new technology.
  • Staff do not trust managers: if workers think their ideas will be used to cut jobs, they stop offering them.

source.verbatim: continuous improvement through many small, regular changes, most of them suggested by the workers who do the job.

cards.front: Define just-in-time (JIT). Evaluate whether a firm should switch from just-in-case to JIT stock management.
cards.back:
Just-in-time (JIT) — a way of managing stock in which materials arrive just as they are needed and products are made to meet orders, so the firm holds little or no buffer stock.

Just-in-case is the alternative: holding buffer stocks of materials and finished goods in case a delivery is late or demand rises.

  • Cash flow: less money tied up in stock → more cash for other uses → less need to borrow.
  • Costs: less storage, and less stock wasted → lower average cost.
  • Risk: one late delivery → no buffer stock to fall back on → production stops → lost output and sales. A sudden rise in demand is hard to meet, and small, frequent deliveries miss out on bulk-buying discounts.

It depends on the firm's suppliers (reliable suppliers close by suit JIT; parts shipped from the other side of the world are more likely to be delayed) and how predictable demand is.

Judgement: JIT suits a firm with reliable local suppliers and steady demand. A firm that relies on distant suppliers, or faces sudden peaks in demand, risks losing more from halted production than it saves on stock.

source.verbatim: a way of managing stock in which materials arrive just as they are needed and products are made to meet orders, so the firm holds little or no buffer stock.

cards.front: Build the chains of reasoning: how can lean production give a firm a competitive advantage, and what decides how long the advantage lasts?
cards.back:
• Lower costs: less waste of stock, time and materials → lower average cost → lower prices to win sales, or wider margins at the same price.
  • Better quality: fewer faults → a reputation for reliability → loyal customers, whose demand is more price inelastic → the firm can charge more.
  • Speed: making to order with little stock → the firm can change its products quickly → it responds to new trends before rivals.

How long it lasts depends on:

  • The cost of getting there: training, new systems and new supplier deals cost money, and the savings take time to arrive.
  • Whether rivals can copy it: lean methods are well known. The advantage lasts only if the firm uses them better, which comes down to its culture and staff.

cards.front: Build the chains of reasoning: how do higher productivity, higher capacity utilisation and lean production each lower a firm's average cost?
cards.back:
• Higher productivity: each worker makes more → the wage bill is shared across more units → lower labour cost per unit.
  • Higher capacity utilisation: more output from the same premises and machines → fixed costs are spread over more units → lower fixed cost per unit.
  • Lean production: less stock, scrap and rework → fewer materials and less time wasted → lower cost per unit.

All three get more output from the same resources. Name which cost each one cuts, rather than just saying "costs fall".

cards.front:
A firm sells 1,000 lamps a month at £15. Lean production cuts its average cost from £10 to £8, and it stays at £8 at every output in this question.

(a) It keeps its price. Calculate revenue and profit before and after. (b) It cuts its price to £13, keeping the same margin on each lamp. Calculate revenue and profit if sales rise to 1,500, and if they rise only to 1,100.
cards.back:
• Before: revenue £15 × 1,000 = £15,000. Profit (£15 − £10) × 1,000 = £5,000.
  • (a) Keeps its price: revenue is still £15,000. Profit (£15 − £8) × 1,000 = £7,000.
  • (b) £13, selling 1,500: revenue £13 × 1,500 = £19,500. Profit (£13 − £8) × 1,500 = £7,500. Demand is price elastic, so revenue rises, and enough extra lamps are sold for the price cut to earn more profit too.
  • (b) £13, selling 1,100: revenue £13 × 1,100 = £14,300, a fall. Profit £5 × 1,100 = £5,500. Demand is price inelastic, so revenue falls, and keeping the price earns more.

Lower costs do not raise revenue on their own. Revenue is price times quantity sold, and neither changes just because costs fall. If the firm keeps its price, the gain shows up in profit. A price cut raises revenue only if demand is price elastic, and only if rivals do not cut their prices too.

Elastic demand guarantees higher revenue, not higher profit. Here the price cut beats the £7,000 from keeping the price only if more than 1,400 lamps are sold (£7,000 ÷ £5).

cards.front: What counts as waste for a firm? Build the chains from cutting waste to lower costs and higher sales, and say what limits the gain.
cards.back:
Waste is anything a firm pays for that adds nothing to what the customer buys: materials thrown away, faulty products that are scrapped or reworked, staff and machines standing idle, energy used heating empty space, and goods made that nobody buys.

  • Costs: less material and energy used per unit → lower variable cost per unit → lower average cost.
  • Sales: a name for cutting waste and packaging → appeals to customers who care about the environment → more sales, and sometimes a higher price.

Firms cut waste with lean methods, products designed to use less material, energy-efficient equipment and more accurate sales forecasts.

The gain is limited by:

  • The up-front cost: new equipment or a redesign pays off only if the savings last long enough.
  • Trade-offs: cutting stock to the minimum raises the risk of running out, and greener materials can cost more than the ones they replace.

cards.front: Define product development lead time. Why does a short one give a firm a competitive advantage?
cards.back:
Product development lead time — the time between starting work on a new product and putting it on sale.

  • First to market: the firm launches before rivals → no direct competition at first → it can charge a high price (price skimming) → higher revenue and profit until rivals arrive.
  • Keeping up with tastes: a toy maker turns a new craze into stock within weeks → it sells what is wanted now → fewer unsold lines and fewer discounts.
  • Lower development costs: fewer months of paying designers and engineers → lower costs, and the R&D spending is earned back sooner.

source.verbatim: the time between starting work on a new product and putting it on sale.

cards.front: A firm cuts its average cost and shortens its product development lead time. Evaluate how far this will raise its sales revenue and profit.
cards.back:
The case for: lower average cost → a lower price, or a wider margin at the same price. A short lead time → first to market, and in step with tastes → higher revenue and fewer discounts.

It depends on:

  • PED: a price cut raises revenue only when demand is price elastic. With inelastic demand, keeping the price and taking the wider margin earns more.
  • Rivals' response: if rivals cut their costs and prices too, nobody gains market share, and the saving passes to consumers.
  • The market: a short lead time matters most where products and tastes change fast, such as clothing and toys. A firm selling salt gains little.
  • Quality: rushing a product out raises the risk of faults, recalls and a damaged brand.

Judgement: the gain is largest for a firm in a fast-changing market, facing price-elastic demand, whose rivals cannot easily match its costs. Where rivals can, the saving soon passes to consumers as lower prices.
